question: How should a stochastic bandit, its learning objective (regret) and the regret decomposition be defined formally?
contributions: Formal definition of the stochastic bandit and its assumptions (4.1)
Environment classes, structured and unstructured (4.3, Table 4.1)

limits: Chapter defines the model only; it gives no algorithm (no epsilon-greedy, UCB, explore-then-commit) and no regret bound. Follow-the-leader appears only as an exercise.
Sub-Gaussian is not defined here: Table 4.1 says it 'will be deﬁned in Chapter 5'.
Regret is defined with respect to expectation, so unsuited to risk measures (Note 4); Bayesian regret deferred to Chapters 34-36; non-stationary bandits deferred to Chapter 31.
Proofs of Lemma 4.4 and Proposition 4.8 are left as exercises; the text says 'the second and last lemmas of the chapter' though Lemmas 4.4-4.6 appear.
practices: Default utility on the cumulative reward is its expected value (risk-neutral), p.57.
Design a policy assuming a known horizon, then adapt to unknown horizon with minimal loss, p.57.
To keep regret small, play an arm with larger suboptimality gap proportionally fewer times (Lemma 4.5), p.62.
Estimate each arm's mean by playing it, then play the largest estimated mean; the question is how often each arm must be played, p.61.
Use pseudo-regret rather than random regret when assessing risk or skill, p.68.
Include error bars when plotting average regret as an estimate of expected regret, p.72.

terms.definition: A stochastic bandit is a collection of distributions ν = (Pa : a ∈A), where A is the set of available actions.

In each round t, the learner chooses At in A; environment samples Xt in R from P_At and reveals it. Assumptions: (a) conditional distribution of Xt given A1,X1,...,At-1,Xt-1,At is P_At; (b) conditional law of At given the past is pi_t(.|A1,X1,...,At-1,Xt-1), so the learner cannot use future observations.
Sn = sum_{t=1}^n Xt
a set of bandits E for which nu in E is guaranteed (the learner's partial knowledge of nu)
A finite and E = {nu=(Pa) : Pa in Ma for all a} = product of Ma; playing a reveals nothing about b != a

Not a product set; learner can obtain information about actions without playing them. Examples: A={1,2}, E={(B(θ),B(1-θ))}; stochastic linear bandit nu_θ=(N(<a,θ>,1): a in A), learnable by playing d spanning actions; graph path-success bandit with B(prod_{e in a} θ_e).
Finite vs infinite number of degrees of freedom needed to describe an element (Bernoulli parametric, subgaussian non-parametric)

Bernoulli {(B(μi))i : μ in [0,1]^k}; Uniform {(U(ai,bi))}; Gaussian known var {(N(μi,σ²))}; Gaussian unknown var; Finite variance {V[X~Pi] <= σ²}; Finite kurtosis (kurtosis = E[(X-E[X])^4]/V[X]^2); Bounded support Supp(Pi) in [a,b]; Subgaussian {Pi is σ-subgaussian for all i}
μa(ν)=∫x dPa(x); μ*(ν)=max_a μa(ν); assumed finite with argmax non-empty
Rn(π,ν) = nμ*(ν) - E[sum_{t=1}^n Xt] (Eq 4.1), expectation under the measure induced by π and ν
BRn(π,Q) = ∫_E Rn(π,ν) dQ(ν) for prior Q on E (Eq 4.4)
Δa(ν) = μ*(ν) - μa(ν), also called action gap or immediate regret; zero for optimal arms
Ta(t) = sum_{s=1}^t I{As = a}, number of times a was chosen after round t; random in general

For any policy π and stochastic bandit environment ν with A finite or countable and horizon n in N, Rn = sum_{a in A} Δa E[Ta(n)]. Proof: insert indicators sum_a I{At=a}=1, get Rn = sum_a sum_t E[(μ*-Xt)I{At=a}], then E[(μ*-Xt)I{At=a}|At] = I{At=a}Δa.
R̂n = nμ* - sum_t Xt
R̄n = nμ* - sum_t μ_{At}
for all ν in E, lim_{n→∞} Rn(π,ν)/n = 0
A sequence (πt) where πt is a probability kernel from (Ω_{t-1},F_{t-1}) to ([k],2^[k])
Independent X_si with law Pi; Xt = X_{t,At} (table), or Xt = X_{T_At(t),At} (stack of rewards per arm, top pulled each time); all give the same law of the outcome
Decision makers who base their decisions on expected values
Chooses each action once then the action with the largest average observed so far, ties random; also 'stay with the winner' or 'greedy algorithm'
E=M1 x {δ_μ2}; once action 2 is played it is played until the end
